column1: Compassus Home Health - Capacity & Scheduling Concept Dictionary
Master glossary of every concept, variable, and definition that shapes home health capacity and scheduling. The Variable Inventory and Functional Scorecard tabs draw from this list.

column3: The total clinical visit work a branch's workforce can deliver over a period, by discipline and by service area, netted against work already committed - the supply ceiling and the open room left in it. Measured in productivity points (or visits) per clinician per day and week, rolled up to branch. A quantity-and-location question: how much can this branch absorb, for which disciplines, in which territories, this week.

The assignment of specific ordered visits to specific clinicians on specific days, and increasingly specific sequences and times, subject to discipline, availability, geography, and patient constraints. An allocation-and-matching question at the single-visit grain: who sees whom, which day, in what order.

Capacity sets the envelope and scheduling fills it. The same underlying data - clinicians, disciplines, territory, availability, visit weights, PTO - is capacity when read as totals and scheduling when read as assignments.

The communication and confirmation work that turns a schedule into delivered care and keeps the board stable - day-before confirmations, reminders, reschedules, coverage on call-outs, care-team updates. It both protects capacity (fewer failed visits) and consumes it (coordination time), so it is called out as its own band that ties the two together.
Reference code. SH = shared spine, C = capacity, S = scheduling.
Which side of the seam the factor sits on - Shared, Capacity, Scheduling, or Coordination (the execution layer). Color-banded down the sheet.
The grouping within a layer (Roster, Geography, Routing, Clinician pattern, Caregiver, Clinical timing, Compliance, Distribution, ...).
The specific capacity or scheduling factor being defined.
Why it matters and how it behaves in practice.

Hard = must be honored or the visit fails (patient refuses mornings; caregiver-present teaching). 
Soft = optimize toward, break under pressure (clinician prefers an 8am start). 
Structural = a fixed property of supply/geography. 
Event = a demand trigger. Derived = computed live. Config = a policy-set constant.

How safely automation can act on the factor without unintended harm to the process, patient, clinician, or branch: High / Medium / Low. Composited from five factors - Legibility (captured in data, or informal knowledge?), Volatility (stable, or easily thrown off by a small error?), Coupling (isolated, or entangled?), Reversibility (recoverable, or lasting harm?), and Harm surface (who is exposed - patient, clinician, or branch?).

The setting implied by the confidence. Control = the system can decide and execute (High). Assist = the system proposes and a person confirms (Medium). Read = the system surfaces information only and a person owns the decision (Low).
Plain-language reason for the confidence and posture on that row.
Optional deeper systems view. Hidden by default - unhide the column for the fuller perspective; keep hidden for team and employer views.
Originating system(s) for the data: HCHB, Workday, Routing, Census, Manual, Config, Derived, or Telephony.

Which of the three target modules the variable is built or bought into - Capacity Management, Scheduling Engine, or Patient Engagement. An extra grouping over the dictionary, not a replacement for Layer or Category.

column5: The count of active clinicians available to deliver visits - the base unit of supply.

column7: 14 RNs, 6 PTs, 3 OTs, 2 SLPs active in the Charleston branch.
column11: Clear roster fact; safe to sync and read.
column12: Fixed point - legible supply fact; encoding it doesn't move the pattern.

column5: The clinical license type that determines which ordered visits a clinician may perform.

column7: A wound-care SOC ordered for RN cannot be filled by an available PT.

column12: Fixed point - hard structural fact.

column5: Classification of a discipline as assessing (can open/evaluate) or assistant (follow-up only).

column12: Fixed point - deterministic from discipline.

column5: Full-time, part-time, per-diem, or contract status.

column11: Clear employment attribute.
column12: Fixed point - structural.

column5: Days a clinician is unavailable (PTO, non-working days, working pattern).

column11: Once entered, a firm blackout the system can honor.
column12: Hard boundary; once in the field it's a clean edge automation can hold.

column5: The geographic area a branch or clinician covers.

column7: Branch covers Berkeley/Dorchester/Charleston; a clinician covers zips 29464/29466/29429/29492.
column11: Territory lines carry local knowledge; propose and confirm.
column12: Zip lines look fixed but encode local knowledge; read and propose, don't redraw.

column5: The point value assigned to each visit type - the common currency of capacity and load.

column7: A day of three SOCs (7.5 pts) nearly fills an FT ceiling; a day of routines does not.
column11: Policy constant; simple lookup.
column12: Config constant - a fixed point.

column5: The expected weekly points and the maximum daily points a clinician should carry.
column6: Target = the load we plan toward; ceiling = the hard cap capacity cannot exceed.
column7: Weekly expected 30 pts; max daily 8 for FT.
column11: Policy constant; simple lookup.
column12: Config constant - a fixed point.

column5: New starts-of-care entering and patients discharging - the events that open and close capacity and schedule slots.

column7: A Thursday discharge in 29461 reopens RN capacity a new referral can fill.
column11: Event detection is clear; the downstream action is scored separately.
column12: Legible trigger; sensing is safe, the response is where judgment enters.

column5: The staffed supply broken out by discipline and FTE type.

column7: 14 FT RNs + 2 PD RNs sets the RN ceiling before any scheduling.
column11: Clear supply fact.
column12: Legible supply - a stable attractor.

column5: The counties the branch is responsible for covering.
column6: Sets the outer boundary of where capacity must exist; gaps here are coverage holes no scheduling can fill.
column7: Branch owns all of Dorchester county regardless of where clinicians live.
column11: Fixed coverage boundary.
column12: Fixed boundary.

column5: The zip codes each clinician is assigned to serve.

column7: RN capacity exists but all of it sits in 29464 while the referral is in 29429.
column11: Neighborhood ownership is partly informal knowledge.
column12: Reachability carries tacit routing knowledge; propose, let humans tune it.

column5: Whether to model coverage at census-tract rather than zip level.

column7: One large zip spans an urban core and a rural edge with very different drive times.
column11: A modeling choice, not a live control; evaluate deliberately.
column12: Granularity choice reshapes both basins at once; decide deliberately, not by default.

column5: Points already booked against a clinician or branch.

column7: RN ceiling 40 pts/week, 32 booked, 8 open.
column11: Derived from booked visits.
column12: Derived - reads the pattern, doesn't move it.

column5: Bookable points left in each day after assigned work.

column7: Wednesday shows 3 open RN points; Thursday shows red.
column11: Direct derivation from the schedule.
column12: Derived read of open room.

column5: Sum of remaining points from today through end of week.
column6: The 'how much can we still take this week' number leaders act on.
column7: 22 bookable RN points remain branch-wide, rest of week.
column11: Direct derivation.
column12: Derived.

column5: Open capacity limited to assessing clinicians of a given discipline.

column7: 6 open RN-assessing points can absorb two SOCs (2.5 each).
column11: Direct derivation, discipline-filtered.
column12: Derived.

column5: Capacity available on demand from per-diem and contract staff.

column7: Two PD RNs each offering 12 visits/week absorb overflow.
column11: Availability is stated; actual engagement depends on the relationship.
column12: Buffer size is legible; whether it flexes is relational - read, don't presume.

column5: Capacity for visits requiring a specific competency beyond discipline.

column7: 14 RNs but only 3 wound-certified; wound capacity is the real constraint.

column12: Competency lives partly in reputation, not credentials; surface it.

column5: Reduced-capacity status of new hires still onboarding.
column6: New clinicians count as headcount but not full capacity; ignoring ramp overstates supply.
column7: A week-2 hire carries a 4-pt ceiling, not 8.
column11: Headcount is clear; the true ramp curve requires judgment.
column12: Ramp is a curve, not a switch - judgment, not a rule.

column5: Off-cycle load carried into the standard week.
column6: Weekend and on-call work reduces the capacity a clinician brings to weekday visits.
column7: A clinician off the weekend rotation starts Monday already partly loaded.
column11: Clear from the rotation log.
column12: Legible load.

column5: The rate of incoming referrals.
column6: Primary demand driver, but held steady by scope decision; documented so capacity math is transparent, not scored as a lever.
column7: Assume a constant referral rate across the evaluation window.
column11: Out of scope; held steady. Surface only.
column12: Held constant; out of scope by choice.

column5: How recently territory assignments were reviewed against actual referral and caseload distribution, and how far apart the two have drifted.
column6: C-03 records what the territory is; this records whether it is still right. Territories are set once on thin data and then left, so drift is invisible until capacity strands in one zip while the next saturates.
column7: One territory carries ~30 patients across two full-time clinicians while the adjacent area turns down starts.
column11: The misalignment is measurable; redrawing a boundary is a leadership act. Propose, never redraw.
column12: The origin variable of the whole model - everything downstream inherits a stale boundary.

column5: The visit types and cadence a patient's plan of care requires.
column6: The demand signal at the visit grain; everything scheduling does is placing these orders into viable slots.
column7: Ordered 2w9: nine visits over two weeks in a set pattern.
column11: Orders are clear in HCHB.
column12: The demand signal - legible.

column5: The specific type of each ordered visit.
column6: Sizes the slot (points) and dictates the required role; SOC/eval must go to assessing staff.
column7: An SOC (2.5) needs an assessing RN and a longer window than a routine (1.0).
column11: Clear order attribute.
column12: Legible.

column5: The date range within which each ordered visit must occur.
column6: A visit placed outside its window is a compliance miss even if delivered; scheduling is bounded by these windows.
column7: The 9th visit of a 2w9 must land before the two-week window closes.
column11: Rule-based date window; ideal to enforce and flag.
column12: Hard, legible clock - safe to enforce.

column5: The days a clinician prefers or is set to work.
column6: Baseline availability; some rotate (baylor, Fri/Mon off) which scheduling must respect.
column7: Clinician works Mon-Thu, off Fridays.
column11: Set pattern, but rotations and swaps are informal.
column12: Pattern with informal exceptions; read, propose.

column5: The time of day a clinician prefers to begin visits.
column6: Anchors the front of the route; some want an 8am first visit, others a later start.
column7: Clinician A always wants an 8am first visit near home.
column11: Capturable preference; confirm before acting.
column12: Preference; capturable but personal - assist, don't fix.

column5: Whether the start time is fixed or can shift day to day.
column6: Distinguishes a rigid clinician from one who moves to accommodate a patient window - a schedulable lever.
column7: Clinician B will start at 7 or 9 depending on the day.
column11: Depends on the clinician's willingness; a wrong assumption damages trust.
column12: Sensitive dependence - a person's willingness; assuming it reshapes the relationship. Read only.

column5: Whether and when a clinician takes a lunch break.
column6: A fixed lunch removes a mid-day slot and splits the route; some take none.
column7: Clinician takes 12-12:30 lunch daily; no visits across it.
column11: Capturable habit.
column12: Personal habit - assist.

column5: Time reserved mid-day for charting.
column6: Consumes schedulable time and shapes the route into segments.
column7: Clinician holds 1-2pm for documentation.
column11: Capturable habit.
column12: Personal habit - assist.

column5: A mid-day gap for errands or childcare, with visits before and after.
column6: Creates a two-cluster day scheduling must build around, not a continuous block.
column7: Sees 3 patients, breaks 2-4pm for school pickup, then 2 more.
column11: Personal daily routine that varies; hard to predict reliably.
column12: The clinician's own daily rhythm - a strange attractor; small control inputs distort it. Read only.

column5: The time by which a clinician must finish.
column6: Caps the back of the route; a hard stop behaves as a hard constraint.
column7: Must end by 4:30 for childcare - no later visits.
column11: Firm once known, but knowing it depends on the clinician telling you.
column12: Firm edge once known; the knowing is tacit.

column5: The most visits a clinician will carry before a break or in a day.
column6: Bounds how densely a day packs regardless of open points.
column7: Caps at 6 visits/day even if points allow more.
column11: Capturable ceiling; confirm.
column12: Personal ceiling - assist.

column5: How readily a clinician bends their pattern on request.
column6: Meta-variable: determines which soft constraints can be overridden under pressure.
column7: Clinician C reliably says yes to an added visit; Clinician D never does.
column11: Relationship-based; automating it can damage the trust it depends on.
column12: Pure relational variable; the act of automating it changes what it measures. Read only.

column5: Willingness to take visits beyond target.
column6: Drives coverage uptake and surge response; often tied to PPV pay.
column7: PPV clinician accepts a 7th visit; salaried declines.
column11: Relationship- and pay-linked; surface it, do not assume.
column12: Relational and pay-linked; surface, never presume.

column5: Where the clinician's day begins and ends.
column6: Anchors first and last visit selection; a distant first visit wastes the day.
column7: Lives in 29466; first visit ideally in or near it.
column11: Clear location anchor.
column12: Legible anchor.

column5: Assigning the ordered visit to a clinician of the required license and role.
column6: Hard gate; wrong discipline cannot deliver the visit.
column7: An RN SOC cannot be assigned to a PTA.
column11: Firm licensure gate, fully clear.
column12: Hard gate - legible.

column5: Assigning visits needing a competency to a qualified clinician.
column6: Narrows the eligible pool below the discipline - a hidden hard constraint.
column7: Only wound-certified RNs are eligible for a complex wound SOC.
column11: Only as good as the competency data, which is often incomplete.
column12: Only as legible as the credential data - often it isn't.

column5: How close a candidate visit is to the clinician's other visits that day.
column6: Primary efficiency lever; clustering cuts drive time and raises effective capacity.
column7: Add the 29445 visit to the clinician already working 29445 Thursday.
column11: Geographic optimization; safe and reversible.
column12: Geometry - safe optimization; the efficiency here is real, not the attractor's slack.

column5: Total drive distance of the sequenced day.
column6: The cost scheduling minimizes; high mileage means fewer visits fit.
column7: Re-sequencing drops the day from 46 to 31 miles.
column11: Deterministic routing math.
column12: Deterministic.

column5: The order visits are performed within the day.
column6: Where time-windowed and caregiver-present visits pin the route and everything else fills around them.
column7: A fixed 10am teaching visit anchors the morning sequence.
column11: Clear, but pinned by fixed time constraints; propose a sequence.
column12: Legible skeleton pinned by tacit anchors; propose, let the human place the anchors.

column5: The time band a visit must fall within.
column6: Converts a day-level order into a time-level constraint - the unit real scheduling increasingly works in.
column7: Visit must occur 9-11am.
column11: Enforceable once captured; capture is the weak point.
column12: Enforceable once captured; capture is where reality leaks in.

column5: Visit-type, territory, or acuity limits on a clinician.
column6: Hard gates set by the scheduler / clinical manager.
column7: 'No wound care; north territory only.'
column11: Documented firm restriction; honor it.
column12: Documented hard gate.

column5: Keeping the same clinician with a patient across the episode.
column6: Improves outcomes and satisfaction; a strong soft preference scheduling protects where possible.
column7: The patient's SOC RN follows through recert.
column11: Prior clinician is known; the relationship's value is informal.
column12: The relationship is load-bearing but invisible in the data; protect it, don't score it away.

column5: Patient request for a same- or specific-gender clinician.
column6: Can be a hard constraint for cultural, religious, or comfort reasons.
column7: Patient requests a female clinician for personal care.
column11: Sensitive; surface and confirm rather than auto-match.
column12: Sensitive; surface and confirm.

column5: Matching clinician language or cultural familiarity to the patient.
column6: Affects teaching effectiveness; sometimes hard when no interpreter is available.
column7: Spanish-speaking patient paired with a bilingual clinician.
column11: Capturable; confirm for teaching-critical visits.
column12: Read and confirm for teaching-critical visits.

column5: Patient refusal of a time band (no early, no morning, no afternoon).
column6: Removes slots and reshapes the whole route, but it is a negotiation rather than a wall - malleable based on relationship, which is exactly why it must be asked rather than assumed.
column7: Patient refuses any visit before 11am.
column11: Firm rule once captured, but a stale refusal causes a failed visit.
column12: Hard once captured, but a stale value fails the visit - the map isn't the territory.

column5: The time the patient prefers to be seen.
column6: Softer than a refusal but drives satisfaction and access.
column7: Patient prefers early afternoon.
column11: Soft window; optimize toward it, confirm.
column12: Soft - optimize toward, confirm.

column5: Days the patient is unavailable due to standing commitments.
column6: Standing dialysis or clinic days block those dates entirely.
column7: At dialysis Mon/Wed/Fri mornings.
column11: Standing commitments are capturable but patient-reported.
column12: Standing constraint; patient-reported, so trust but verify.

column5: Visit can only occur when a caregiver is present.
column6: Ties the visit to a second person's calendar; common for teaching (wound care, insulin) and safety.
column7: Wound-care teaching only when the daughter is home, evenings.
column11: Firm requirement, but the input is informal and changing, with patient-safety impact.
column12: Danger quadrant - hard rule, fluctuating tacit input, patient harm. The clearest 'read, never control.'

column5: Patient cognition requires a caregiver present or specific conditions.
column6: Makes caregiver availability a hard gate and narrows viable windows sharply.
column7: Dementia patient can't admit a clinician alone; caregiver home only 8-10am.
column11: Cognition plus caregiver dependency; system surfaces, a person decides.
column12: Danger quadrant - cognition plus caregiver dependency; automation must only surface.

column5: The caregiver's own changing availability.
column6: Scheduling around two moving calendars - the hardest real-world case.
column7: Caregiver works rotating shifts; the available window changes weekly.
column11: Two changing calendars, largely undocumented; needs a person.
column12: Two moving calendars, undocumented - the purest sensitive dependence in the system.

column5: Visit timing dictated by clinical need.
column6: Fasting labs AM, insulin/meal-timed visits, wound-care cadence; timing is clinical, not preference.
column7: Insulin-teaching visit must align with the patient's morning dose.
column11: Clinical timing judgment with patient-safety impact; flag, do not decide.
column12: Clinical judgment with patient harm; flag, never decide.

column5: The patient's other appointments that block windows or days.
column6: Dialysis, infusion, MD visits remove time; must be known to avoid failed visits.
column7: No PT visit Tuesday - patient has an all-day infusion.
column11: Capturable if reported, but often surfaces only in conversation.
column12: Surfaces in conversation, not the record; read and confirm.

column5: Higher-acuity patients requiring a more skilled or specific clinician.
column6: Raises the match bar and can force a specific individual.
column7: High-acuity cardiac patient needs the cardiac-competent RN.
column11: Acuity-to-skill is clinical judgment; recommend, a person confirms.
column12: Clinical judgment; recommend, the human owns it.

column5: Ordering visits to manage infection risk.
column6: Immunocompromised seen first, infectious last - a sequencing constraint on the day.
column7: See the neutropenic patient before the C. diff patient.
column11: Partly rule-based; confirm for complex cases.
column12: Partly a rule, partly judgment; assist.

column5: The window in which a start-of-care must occur after referral.
column6: A hard regulatory clock; a late SOC is a compliance and quality failure.
column7: SOC must occur within 48 hours of referral acceptance.
column11: Regulatory clock, fully clear - the safest automation win.
column12: Hard regulatory clock - the safest thing to automate.

column5: Windows for recertification and required face-to-face encounters.
column6: Bounds when certain visits can and must be scheduled.
column7: Recert visit must fall in the last 5 days of the episode.
column11: Regulatory window; enforce and flag.
column12: Regulatory - enforce.

column5: Required RN supervision of LPN/aide on a cadence.
column6: Chains one clinician's schedule to another's - a dependency, not a single assignment.
column7: RN supervisory visit due every 14 days for the aide's patient.
column11: Rule-based cadence dependency; clear and enforceable.
column12: Rule-based cadence; legible.

column5: Rebooking past-dated visits that were never worked.
column6: The recovery loop; unaddressed, these become compliance and revenue misses.
column7: Wednesday's unworked visit must be rebooked by Friday.
column11: Detecting the miss is straightforward; choosing the reschedule pulls in every soft constraint.
column12: Sensing the miss is legible; the reschedule pulls the whole basin back in - assist.

column5: Required notes when a visit is missed.
column6: Compliance artifact tied to the exception.
column7: Missed-visit note completed for the skipped Thursday visit.
column11: Workflow and compliance prompt and tracking.
column12: Workflow - safe.

column5: Concentrating visits early in the week.
column6: Protects against end-of-week misses; 42% Mon-Tue share is the gold standard.
column7: Schedule builds toward 42% of weekly points by Tuesday night.
column11: Optimize toward the target, but forcing it disrupts clinician routines.
column12: A target, not a law; forcing it flattens the clinician's rhythm into a fixed point.

column5: Whether a clinician is on track against their own planned schedule to date.
column6: Signals when to rebalance the rest of the week.
column7: By Wednesday the clinician is at 70% of planned-to-date - behind.
column11: Derived metric; safe to surface.
column12: Derived read.

column5: Spreading load so no single day is over- or under-packed.
column6: Prevents both burnout days and idle days; smooths the week against the ceiling.
column7: Move one Thursday visit to a light Monday.
column11: Optimizable, but it touches human routines and informal constraints.
column12: Optimizable, but it touches human routines - assist, don't dictate.

column5: Whether authorization exists for an ordered visit, how many visits the payer permits to be scheduled against pending authorization, and what gates further authorization.
column6: The largest single bottleneck identified in the whiteboard session. A referral clears authorization verification before scheduling sees it at all, and the pending-auth allowance caps how far ahead the scheduler can work.
column7: Payer permits three visits against pending auth; the ordered frequency is 2w1, so the scheduler cannot plot past week two.
column11: Auth state is a firm gate once known, but chasing it is relational and payer rules vary by state - surface the gate, let a person work the exception.
column12: A wait the current process map does not show. State-specific auth rules belong in the system knowledge base; they feed capacity forecasting directly.

column5: Any order written after the 485 is submitted, and whether it changes visit frequency.
column6: In steady state there is no recurring scheduler workflow unless an add-on order changes frequency - at which point the order routes through DCS approval, then authorization, then back to the scheduler.
column7: Physician adds wound care 3w2 in week three; the plan re-enters the queue for every affected discipline.
column11: Detecting the order is clean; the frequency change pulls the whole assignment basin back in.
column12: The mechanism by which a settled plan re-enters the queue. Bottleneck awaiting DCS workflow.

column5: Market-specific safety rules that constrain when and where a visit may be scheduled, and the alerts a clinician must see before the visit.
column6: Safety requirements vary by market and are not preferences. One market requires screening questions on firearms in the home, other people present, and mental illness, instituted after a clinician was killed in a patient's home.
column7: No unaccompanied visits in a named area after 4pm; the slot is removed from the route, not flagged for override.
column11: A hard rule once captured, but capture is manual and market-local - honour it, let a person own the exception.
column12: Constrains time-of-day and geography, and bounds where an automated agent may substitute for a person at all.

column5: The first visit time a clinician can actually secure with their current caseload, as distinct from the time they prefer (S-05), and the gap between the two.
column6: S-05 records the preference. Nothing records whether it is being achieved. The gap is the clearest measure of autonomy lost to the caseload rather than to management - and it is invisible today.
column7: Clinician prefers an 8am start; the earliest slot any patient will accept is 10am. Two hours of the day are gone and nobody owns it.
column11: Read, deliberately. Inferring preference from observed start times records defeat as choice and then optimises to preserve it. Ask, record, report the gap as a problem to work.
column12: A clinician at 10am by choice and one at 10am by patient refusal look identical in the data, and they are opposite situations.

column5: Whether an active power of attorney holds legal authority to sign admission consents and to be the contact of record.
column6: Distinct from a caregiver-present requirement. Where a POA exists the patient's own agreement does not satisfy consent, and some POAs direct that the patient not be contacted at all.
column7: Nurse arrives for the SOC; the patient cannot sign and the POA is two states away. The visit is wasted.
column11: A legal fact once captured, but capture is manual and it changes - surface it before the visit is booked and let a person confirm who may be contacted.
column12: Discovering it at the door wastes a start-of-care visit; contacting the wrong party is both a service failure and a disclosure problem.

column5: A patient's assessed risk of rehospitalization, used to prioritise visit timing and avoid care gaps.
column6: A scheduling input, not only a clinical one. It should decide which visits survive a call-out and which patients tolerate a gap. The natural companion to S-33 acuity, which helps with coverage triage.
column7: Two visits compete for one covering clinician; the higher-risk patient keeps the slot.
column11: A risk score may inform priority; it may not silently reorder a clinician's day or override clinical judgment.
column12: Open question: whether Pulse exposes this at patient level in a form scheduling can consume.

column5: Depth and age of the plan-of-care QA queue and the physician-order approval queue.
column6: Plan-of-care QA is a hard stop: visits cannot be scheduled until it clears. When the queue is behind, an assistant waits on visits and days of care compress into one. It is a live scheduling constraint that nobody downstream can see.
column7: QA queue runs four days behind; the aide's first three visits collapse into one week.
column11: Queue depth is countable, but the queue is other people's work - put it in front of the people it blocks, do not reorder it.
column12: Order approval is an HCHB toggle rather than a Medicare requirement, and its queue is the largest source of add-on order delay.

column5: Elapsed time between a visit occurring and the clinician syncing its documentation, during which visit state is unknown to the back office.
column6: Delivered over Citrix, the back office can see only that a visit was started or is incomplete. A visit performed Tuesday may not sync until Friday and reads as undocumented; conversely a started visit is not always a completed one.
column7: A clinician who called 911 has started a visit that did not happen; the schedule still shows it as worked.
column11: Measure the blind window and report it. Nothing may depend on real-time visit state read out of HCHB.
column12: Any capacity or exception logic built on real-time visit state will be wrong, and the size of that error is measurable.

column5: Contacting the patient ahead of the visit to confirm it will happen.
column6: The single biggest reducer of failed and no-show visits; today largely a manual clinician or office task.
column7: Clinician calls Thursday evening to confirm Friday's 9am visit.
column11: Confirmation cuts failed visits; the call can surface changes, so prompt and let a person confirm.
column12: Protects scheduled capacity; the human touch catches what a reminder can't - assist, don't fully automate.

column5: System-sent call, text, or email reminders of upcoming visits.
column6: A safe, high-value automation that cuts no-shows without consuming human time.
column7: Automated text at 5pm: your nurse visit is tomorrow around 9am.
column11: Rule-based reminder dispatch - a clean automation win.
column12: Legible, low-risk - the reminder is deterministic; safe to control.

column5: Notifying the patient the clinician is on the way.
column6: Improves access and satisfaction; fully derivable from the live route.
column7: Auto-text: your therapist is about 20 minutes away.
column11: Derived from the live route; safe to automate.
column12: Deterministic from position and route - a clean control automation.

column5: Outbound welcome call to a newly referred patient.
column6: Sets expectations and confirms the first visit; often the first coordination touch.
column7: Office calls the new SOC patient to introduce the clinician and confirm timing.
column11: Automate the trigger; the call itself is human and relational.
column12: Automate the trigger, keep the human on the line - assist.

column5: Tracking and honoring how each patient prefers to be reached - text, call, or email.
column6: Determines whether reminders and confirmations even land; a preference the system must store and honor.
column7: Patient opts for text only; no automated calls.
column11: Capturable preference; confirm it for reliability-critical messages.
column12: A capturable channel preference - honor it, don't assume.

column5: Confirming patient and required-caregiver availability before the visit is placed.
column6: Prevents booking into windows that will fail; leans on the caregiver-availability constraints.
column7: Scheduler confirms the daughter is home Tue 8-10am before booking the teaching visit.
column11: Depends on fluctuating patient and caregiver windows; surface, a person owns it.
column12: Feeds off the caregiver sensitive-dependence variables - read, never presume.

column5: Negotiating a new time when the patient or caregiver cannot make the planned visit.
column6: Relational and judgment-heavy; a system can propose slots but the negotiation is human.
column7: Patient cancels Friday; clinician works out Saturday morning with the family.
column11: Relational negotiation; the system can propose slots, a person owns the outcome.
column12: Human negotiation around a moving constraint - read or assist at most.

column5: Following up after a missed visit to reschedule and document it.
column6: The recovery loop; unaddressed misses become compliance and revenue losses.
column7: Patient not home Wednesday; office follows up and rebooks Thursday.
column11: Detecting the miss is clean; the rebooking pulls in every soft constraint.
column12: Detection legible; recovery pulls the whole basin back in - assist.

column5: Finding coverage when a clinician calls out.
column6: Hinges on who will actually say yes; ties directly to per-diem/flex capacity and clinician elasticity.
column7: An RN calls out Monday; the scheduler works the per-diem list to cover the visits.
column11: Coverage hinges on relational willingness; surface options, a person works it.
column12: Runs on the same relational elasticity as per-diem uptake - read/assist.

column5: Sequencing and spacing visits from different disciplines per the plan of care.
column6: Prevents two clinicians arriving together, or a patient over-visited one day and idle the next.
column7: Space the RN and PT visits across the week rather than both on Monday.
column11: Rule-informed but pinned by patient tolerance and clinician routes; propose.
column12: Optimizable only within the limits human tolerance sets - assist.

column5: Keeping the case manager and office in sync on schedule changes.
column6: The connective communication that keeps the record and the team aligned; today the coordination-note habit.
column7: Scheduler notes the visit moved and flags the case manager.
column11: Logging and notification are automatable; what to escalate is human judgment.
column12: Notification is safe; the escalation judgment is human - assist.

column5: The non-visit time clinicians and schedulers spend coordinating.
column6: The capacity face of coordination: this time reduces visit capacity and caps a scheduler's span.
column7: A clinician spends roughly 45 minutes a day coordinating - capacity that is not visits.
column11: Measure and surface it; the coordination work itself stays human.
column12: The capacity cost of coordination - read and measure, don't control the people doing it.

column5: The verified phone number and reachable channel for the patient and, where applicable, the caregiver or POA - including which party is the correct contact for scheduling.
column6: Every coordination function depends on reaching the right person on a working number, and today that detail is scattered. Distinct from CO-05, which is channel preference; a preference is no use without a verified number for the right party.
column7: Reminder texts go to a disconnected mobile while the daughter who books every visit is never contacted.
column11: A verified number is a deterministic record the system can hold and dial.
column12: Patient scheduling runs on phone and text. Email is not a patient scheduling channel and should not be designed as one.

column5: Which contact channels are legally permitted - text messaging, and sharing information with family or caregivers - and whether the relevant consent has been signed.
column6: A legal gate rather than a preference, and therefore distinct from CO-05. Consents are signed at the start-of-care visit, so no automated texting can precede admission and the readiness call is necessarily a voice call.
column7: Automated reminder texts begin the day the SOC consent is signed, not the day the referral arrives.
column11: The system must refuse the channel until consent is signed - enforce it, never weigh it.
column12: Any automated outreach built without this gate is a compliance exposure. Outbound automated calling is separately regulated; at least one state treats a call not manually triggered by a human as a robocall.
